title: The Woman Who Asked for Trees

pages.text: Mr Ohene held up a poster of a woman planting a tree surrounded by smiling women. “This,” he said, “is Professor Wangari Maathai of Kenya, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004, not for fighting a war, but for planting trees.” Rita’s hand shot up. “Planting trees for a prize?” she asked. “Listen,” said Mr Ohene. “Her story begins with a girl from a village.”

“Planting trees for a prize?” she asked.
“Listen,” said Mr Ohene.

pages.text: Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in Nyeri, in Kenya. She studied biology in the United States, earned her master’s degree in 1966 and, in 1971, became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, from the University of Nairobi. She later became head of a university department, again the first woman to do so. “She never stopped learning,” said Mr Ohene. “But the story does not stay in a laboratory.”
sentences: Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in Nyeri, in Kenya.
She studied biology in the United States, earned her master’s degree in 1966 and, in 1971, became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, from the University of Nairobi.
She later became head of a university department, again the first woman to do so.
“She never stopped learning,” said Mr Ohene.
“But the story does not stay in a laboratory.”
pages.alt: A woman in graduation robes stands in front of a university with books in her arms.

pages.text: “In the 1970s,” Mr Ohene said, “Maathai travelled in rural Kenya and listened to women. They said that, unlike in the past, they could not meet their basic needs. Among the needs they named were firewood, clean drinking water, balanced diets, shelter and income. She linked these problems to damage to the environment. In her own Nobel lecture she remembered a childhood stream that has since dried up. So she suggested something simple: plant trees.” Rita frowned. “Just plant trees?” she asked. “Just plant trees, with the women’s own hands,” said Mr Ohene.

pages.alt: A woman scientist listens to a circle of rural women beside a dry stream bed.

pages.text: The idea grew into the Green Belt Movement. Women’s groups raised seedlings in nurseries and planted them on farms, schools and church compounds. Nursery groups were given a small payment, reported to be less than ten United States cents, for each seedling that was planted and survived. “It gave women work and a voice,” said Mr Ohene. “And it spread. Other African countries began their own movements.”

pages.alt: Women water seedlings in a nursery with rows of small trees in tins and bags.

pages.text: “How many trees?” asked a boy. Mr Ohene smiled. “That depends on who is counting. The Nobel Prize biography says more than twenty million. Her Nobel lecture in 2004 says more than thirty million. The movement’s own 2011 report says more than fifty-one million. The count grew as the years passed, and every tree was planted by hand.” He looked at the class. “In her Nobel lecture, Maathai said that people who protect the environment, promote democracy and defend human rights ‘plant seeds of peace’. When you quote someone in an essay, copy the exact words.”

pages.text: In 2002 she was elected to Kenya’s parliament, and in 2004 she received the Nobel Peace Prize for her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace. She died on 25 September 2011. “She was not perfect, and nobody is,” said Mr Ohene. “But she showed that one idea, shared with others, can change a country.”

pages.text: That afternoon, Rita and her classmates planted twelve seedlings along the school fence. They gave each one a label with a name, watered them and made a watering rota for the dry season. “We may be the generation that sees them grow,” said Rita. “And the next generation will sit under them.” She patted the soil. “Grow well,” she whispered.

pages.text: Rita wrote a biography paragraph. “Wangari Maathai was born in Nyeri, Kenya, in 1940. She became a scientist and, in 1971, the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate. After listening to rural women, she started a tree-planting movement that grew across Kenya. In 2004, she won the Nobel Peace Prize. She is remembered as a woman who proved that ordinary people can change the land.” The end.

pages.alt: A girl writes a short biography at her desk beside a seedling.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a biography paragraph is written in the third person and mostly in the past tense. It gives dates and facts in order, links them with words such as “after”, “later” and “in 2004”, and ends with a short judgement about the person. Rita did not use “I” in the paragraph. Check each date against your source before you write it. The end.
